narration.text: Python.
Python was created in 1991 by Guido van Rossum,
a Dutch programmer who wanted to make coding easier and
more readable.
At that time, most programming languages were
complex and intimidating,
filled with symbols and strict rules.
Guido wanted a language where developers could focus on thinking, not syntax. Python
took a different path. It's clean and simple syntax almost reads like plain English, which made it extremely beginner-friendly.
This simplicity helped Python grow rapidly across the world,
but Python is not
just for beginners.
It is widely used in data science,
machine learning, artificial intelligence, automation, and back-end
web development. Companies
use Python to analyze massive data sets, train AI models, automate workflows, and build scalable systems. Its
huge library ecosystem allows
developers to build powerful applications without starting from zero. However,
Python has weaknesses. Since it is an interpreted language, it runs slower than compiled languages like C or C++.
It also consumes more memory, making it unsuitable for performance-critical systems like game engines or
operating systems.
Still, for productivity, learning speed, and real-world problem-solving, Python remains one of the most important languages today.
C. C was created in 1972 by
Dennis Ritchie at Bell
Labs.
It was designed to build operating systems, especially Unix, at a time when computers were extremely limited in
power.
What makes C special is how close it is to the hardware.
It gives programmers direct control over memory and system resources.
This results in extremely fast and efficient programs. Because of this, C is still widely used in operating systems, embedded systems, firmware, and low-level
software,
but this power comes with responsibility. C requires manual memory
management, meaning developers must allocate
and free memory themselves.
Even small mistakes can lead to crashes, memory leaks, or serious security vulnerabilities.
C also lacks modern safety features. Despite
this,
learning C teaches how computers actually work at the
lowest level. C++.
C++ was created in the early 1980s by Bjarne
Stroustrup as an extension of C.
His goal was to add object-oriented programming while keeping C's speed and control.
C++ became the backbone of performance-critical software.
It is heavily used in game engines, real-time systems, operating systems, browsers, and financial trading platforms.
Game engines rely on C++ because it allows precise control over performance and memory.
However,
C++ is famously difficult.
The language is large, complex, and easy to misuse.
Memory management is still challenging,
and debugging can be painful,
but when maximum performance and control are required,
C++ remains one of the most powerful tools available. Java. Java was introduced in 1995 by James
Gosling and his
team at Sun Microsystems.
The main idea behind Java was simple: write
once, run anywhere. Instead
of running directly on hardware, Java runs on a virtual machine.
This allows the same Java program to run on different operating systems without modification.
This portability made Java extremely popular in enterprise systems, banking software, large back-end applications, and Android development.
Java automatically manages memory using garbage collection,
which reduces certain types of bugs.
However, Java is often criticized for being verbose.
Simple tasks require a lot of boilerplate code.
Performance is good, but still slower than low-level languages
due to virtual machine overhead.
Despite this, Java remains a core language for large-scale, long-term software systems.
JavaScript. JavaScript was created in 1995 by
Brendan Eich while working at Netscape.
Surprisingly, it was written in just
about 10 days.
Its original purpose was simple:
add interactivity to web pages.
Over time, JavaScript grew far beyond that role.
It is now the only language that runs natively in web browsers.
Every modern website depends on JavaScript for animations, forms, dynamic content, and user interaction.
With the introduction of server-side runtimes,
JavaScript also moved to back-end development, enabling full-stack applications.
JavaScript is powerful, but messy.
Its loose typing, strange edge cases, and asynchronous behavior often confuse developers. Despite these problems,
JavaScript is unavoidable. If
you work on the web, you work with JavaScript. TypeScript.
TypeScript was created by
Anders Hejlsberg
at Microsoft.
It was designed to fix JavaScript's biggest problems without replacing it.
TypeScript adds static typing on top of JavaScript,
allowing developers to catch many errors during development instead of at runtime.
This makes large codebases easier to scale and maintain. Today, most serious web applications use TypeScript.
The downside is added complexity.
Developers must learn types and compilation steps,
but for large projects,
TypeScript has become the standard way to write safe and maintainable JavaScript.
Lua.
Lua was created in the early 1990s by Roberto
Ierusalimschy and
his team in Brazil. It
was designed to be lightweight, fast,
and easy to embed inside other programs.
Lua is widely used
in game development, game engines,
and embedded systems. Many
games use
Lua for scripting game
play logic while the core engine is written in faster languages like C or C++.
Lua's clean syntax makes it easy to learn and modify.
Lua is rarely used alone for large applications.
Its real strength lies in acting as a scripting layer that gives flexibility and control to bigger systems.
Go lang. Go lang was created at
Google by Rob
Pike, Ken Thompson, and Robert Griesemer.
Their goal was to build a language that was simple, fast, and perfect for large-scale back-end systems.
Go lang removes unnecessary complexity and focuses on clarity.
Its built-in support for concurrency makes it ideal for servers, cloud platforms, and distributed systems.
Many modern infrastructure tools and back-end services are written in Go lang. The trade-off
is flexibility. Go
lang intentionally limits features, which can feel restrictive,
but for scalable and reliable systems, Go lang is extremely effective.
Rust. Rust was created by
Graydon Hoare at Mozilla
to solve one major problem, memory safety. It aims
to deliver the performance of C and C++ without their most dangerous bugs. Rust
uses a strict ownership system that catches memory errors at compile time.
This prevents issues like null pointer crashes and data races before the program runs. Rust is now used in operating
systems,
browsers,
and critical infrastructure. Rust
has a steep learning curve.
Its rules can feel overwhelming at first, and compilation times can be slow,
but for developers who want performance and safety, Rust represents the future of systems programming.
